stories.take:
ESPN reports that Quinn Hughes, the former Canucks captain, was booed by the Rogers Arena crowd as he took the ice for warmups in his return to Vancouver with the Wild.

The booing is easy to understand, because the player they're booing keeps driving play. Hughes has 14 points in 12 games so far this season, only 2 of them goals, and he plays 27.03 minutes a night. Our numbers say his own chance quality is close to his results: he has 2.18 expected goals (the quality of his shots) against 2 actual goals. At 5-on-5, MIN takes 63 percent of the expected goals with him on the ice, and his team does 13.9 percentage points better with him out there than without him. That is a big part of why MIN sits at 7-3-2 and holds 58 percent of expected goals overall. VAN, at 2-9-1, takes only 38 percent of the chances, so the crowd has a lot more to be upset about than one departure. Daniel Wagner of Pass it to Bulis posted that "the dead-eyed gremlin always has the puck," which is a fair summary of what the data shows.

Per ESPN, the Hurricanes and restricted free agent defenseman Alexander Nikishin have agreed to a one-year, $3M deal, ending a monthslong standoff. Daily Faceoff adds that he skipped training camp and reportedly asked for a trade after helping Carolina win the Stanley Cup last spring.

The Hurricanes haven't needed him to get started. At 9-2-2 with 20 points through 13 games, CAR owns 60.9% of the expected goals so far this season. Expected goals measures the quality of chances each side creates, so that share says Carolina has controlled play, and the 59% at five-on-five shows it isn't a special-teams mirage. The penalty kill is allowing just 0.52 expected goals per game, which makes it a strength. Our numbers also show goals scored running slightly below expectation (-0.4), so the results aren't flattering the team. If anything, they've been a touch light.

That makes Nikishin's return an addition to a team already playing well, not a rescue. We'd watch how quickly he settles back into the lineup after missing camp, and whether the penalty kill, already strong, gets deeper with him on the ice.

The bigger story is the team he's leaving. VAN sits at 2-9-1 with 5 points through 12 games, and the numbers suggest the record is not just bad luck. Their share of expected goals, which measures the quality of chances taken versus allowed, is 38 percent so far this season, and 40 percent at five-on-five, so they are being outplayed in the flow of the game. The goaltending has made it worse: goals saved above expected, which compares the goals a goalie allowed to what the shot quality predicted, is minus 8.8. Meanwhile their skaters have scored 6.1 more goals than expected, which means the offence is running ahead of its chances. If that fades, the picture gets bleaker. The special teams offer little cover either, with the power play generating 0.47 expected goals per game and the penalty kill allowing 0.98. A roster move like this won't change any of that on its own.

So far this season, NYR sit at 7-5-1 with 15 points and a 51.9% share of expected goals (the share of shot quality they create compared with what they allow). Their goalies have saved 3.6 goals above expected, meaning they've stopped more shots than the quality of those chances would predict. That lifts results a bit, and it's a number to watch if it fades. Offense is the bigger gap: NYR are 1.7 goals below expected, so they're scoring less than their chances deserve. A goalie signing won't change that, but it covers the position if the current tandem falters or gets hurt.

The numbers say the Devils needed this. NJD sit at 7-4-0 with 14 points, and they have controlled play so far this season, with a 60 percent share of expected goals (a measure of chance quality, where 50 is even). The results trail the play, though. They are 4.7 goals below what their chances should have produced, and their goaltending is 5 goals below expected by goals saved above expected, which compares saves made to saves a typical goalie would make on the same shots. A goalie who stops the shots he should is the missing piece.

WPG are the reverse. They are 4-3-3 with 46 percent of expected goals, yet their goaltending is 5.6 goals above expected. That is a team getting more from its goalie than its play has earned, so the Jets' record may be hard to hold without him.
